**The Dread of Umbrathal, the Siren Leviathan**

Beneath the ink-black waters of the Sunless Trench, where light has never touched and pressure crushes bones like glass, *Umbrathal* stirs. This whale is no gentle giant—it is a cathedral of flesh, its body riddled with barnacle-covered mouths that whisper in forgotten dialects. Its eyes are absent, replaced by pulsing voids that see into memory.

Umbrathal was born when a whaling crew slaughtered a pod beneath a blood moon, their greed echoing through the abyss. The sea answered. It stitched the dead into one, a leviathan of vengeance and sorrow. Now it rises only when the ocean is still, its song a low, mournful hum that infects dreams and draws ships off course.

It feeds on *remembrance*. Survivors speak of hallucinations—lost lovers beckoning from the waves, childhood homes glimpsed in the mist—before the hull splits and the sea drinks them whole. name: Larinioides sclopetarius
description:
Larinioides sclopetarius (Clerck, 1757) — Bridge Orbweaver

This 3D model depicts a male Larinioides sclopetarius specimen, collected in Scarborough, Ontario, Canada in 2025. It was reconstructed from a dissected specimen to highlight details of this widespread orbweaving spider.

Textures & Workflow:
Surface textures were created using a hybrid method—combining procedural generation with stencils from high-resolution images captured via a 12MP Raspberry Pi camera mounted on a vintage JENA stereoscope.

Species Overview:
Native to Europe and now common in North America, especially near bridges and waterfronts, L. sclopetarius builds orb-shaped webs and thrives in urban environments. Males are smaller and more mobile, especially during mating season.

Use & Availability:
This model supports education and outreach on Canadian spider diversity.

Available for purchase.
For licensing or inquiries, please contact the artist/seller.

name: Northfield Historical Society Mastodon Tooth
description:
This 3D scan is the result of a collaboration between the Science Museum of Minnesota and the good people of [Northfield Historical Society](http://https://www.northfieldhistory.org/) in Northfield, Minnesota. 

This tooth is one of the few mastodon fossils in the record that we know for sure was discovered in Minnesota. It has research value to the Science Museum of Minnesota, and the folks at Northfield Historical Society were generous and willing to allow their mastodon tooth to be 3D scanned by me. 
Thank you, [Northfield Historical Society!](http://https://www.instagram.com/northfieldhistorical/) 

Specimen Number 1980.15.01. This fossil was discovered in 1918 by a man named Leslie Shaw in "Mr. Cody's Gravel Pit" outside of Dundas, Minnesota. It sat in Mr. Shaw's living room for a few years before being taken to Professor Osborn of Hamline University in 1929. Professor Osborn Identified the fossil as a [mastodon](http://https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastodon) tooth. 100 years later: we agree!

description: Iguanodon (/ɪˈɡwɑːnədɒn/ i-GWAH-nə-don; meaning 'iguana-tooth'), named in 1825, is a genus of iguanodontian dinosaur. Iguanodon was a large, bulky herbivore, measuring up to 9–11 metres (30–36 ft) in length and 4.5 metric tons (5.0 short tons) in body mass.
